subjective.topic: Introduction to Agricultural Biotechnology
subjective.question: Define agricultural biotechnology. What is its scope in crop improvement?
subjective.answer: Agricultural biotechnology is the application of scientific techniques — including genetic engineering, molecular markers, molecular diagnostics, vaccines and plant tissue culture — to modify plants (and other living organisms) for agricultural purposes. Agriculture has been practiced for more than 8,000–10,000 years, but biotechnology has made improvement far faster and more precise than selection and conventional breeding alone. Its scope includes developing crops with higher yield, pest and disease resistance, tolerance to drought, salinity and other stresses, improved nutritional and seed quality, and the production of vaccines and other useful products from plants.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Agricultural Biotechnology
subjective.question: The benefits of biotechnology are summed up as “Heal the World, Fuel the World and Feed the World”. Explain each of these three benefits.
subjective.answer: 1) Heal the World: Biotechnology improves health care and the environment — it produces cheaper, safer and better vaccines and medicines, molecular diagnostics for accurate detection of crop, livestock and human diseases, and helps reduce the use of harmful chemicals, contributing to environmental protection. 2) Fuel the World: Plant biomass and agricultural residues are converted by biotechnological processes into biofuels such as bioethanol and biodiesel, providing renewable alternatives to fossil fuels. 3) Feed the World: Biotechnology increases food production and quality through pest-resistant, disease-resistant and stress-tolerant crops, better yields, improved nutritional value and longer shelf life, helping to meet the food demand of a growing population.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Agricultural Biotechnology
subjective.question: Write a brief history of agricultural biotechnology, from traditional selection to modern genetic engineering.
subjective.answer: Agriculture began more than 8,000–10,000 years ago when humans started domesticating plants. The earliest improvement method was SELECTION — saving seed from the best plants year after year. This was followed by planned BREEDING (hybridization), in which two parents are crossed to combine desirable characters, although it is slow and limited to sexually compatible species. In the twentieth century, plant TISSUE CULTURE showed that plant cells are totipotent and whole plants can be regenerated in vitro (the standard MS medium was introduced by Murashige and Skoog in 1962). The discovery of restriction enzymes, plasmids and the natural gene-transfer system of Agrobacterium tumefaciens led to GENETIC ENGINEERING in the 1980s, allowing a single desired gene to be transferred across species barriers; the first transgenic plants were produced in 1983. In 1990 the first food product of biotechnology — the enzyme chymosin used in cheese production — reached the market. Modern agricultural biotechnology combines genetic engineering with molecular markers, diagnostics and tissue culture for rapid, precise crop improvement.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Agricultural Biotechnology
subjective.question: What advantages do biotechnologically produced vaccines have over traditional vaccines?
subjective.answer: Biotechnological (recombinant/subunit) vaccines are cheaper to produce, better in quality and safer than traditional vaccines because they contain only the protective antigen rather than the whole pathogen, so there is no risk of the vaccine strain causing disease. They are also stable at room temperature and do not need refrigerated storage (cold chain), which makes them much easier to transport and use in the field.

subjective.topic: Genetic and Molecular Markers
subjective.question: What are genetic markers? List the properties of an ideal genetic marker.
subjective.answer: A genetic marker is any phenotypic or molecular difference controlled by genes that can be used to study inheritance, identify individuals or species, and follow a trait of interest in breeding. The three main types are morphological markers, biochemical markers and DNA-based (molecular) markers. An ideal genetic marker should be: (1) highly polymorphic, so that many variants exist; (2) reproducible, giving the same result every time; (3) co-dominant, so heterozygotes can be distinguished from homozygotes; (4) multi-allelic; (5) neutral, with no effect on the phenotype of the plant; (6) free of epistasis and environmental influence; and (7) abundant and evenly distributed over the genome.

subjective.topic: Genetic and Molecular Markers
subjective.question: Describe the three types of molecular markers: morphological, biochemical and DNA-based markers.
subjective.answer: 1) Morphological markers are visible phenotypic differences such as plant height, leaf shape and colour or flower colour, controlled by genes. They need no laboratory work but are few in number. 2) Biochemical markers are protein-based markers, mainly isozymes — different forms of the same enzyme that can be separated by electrophoresis. They are co-dominant but limited in number and influenced by tissue and environment. 3) DNA-based markers detect differences directly in the DNA sequence, e.g. RFLP, RAPD, AFLP, SSR (microsatellites) and SNP markers. They are unlimited in number, unaffected by environment or developmental stage, and can be scored at any stage of the plant's life, so they are the most widely used markers in crop improvement.

subjective.topic: Genetic and Molecular Markers
subjective.question: Give the advantages and limitations of morphological markers.
subjective.answer: Advantages: they are simple to score by visual identification, need no instruments or chemicals, and cost nothing extra during field evaluation. Properties/limitations: they generally express late in the development of the organism, exhibit dominance (heterozygotes cannot be distinguished), exhibit pleiotropy and deleterious effects, show epistasis, are strongly influenced by the environment, and are very few in number — so they are of limited use in modern breeding programmes.

subjective.topic: Genetic and Molecular Markers
subjective.question: What are AFLP markers? Outline the basic steps of the AFLP technique.
subjective.answer: AFLP (Amplified Fragment Length Polymorphism) is a DNA-based marker technique that combines restriction digestion with PCR. Steps: (1) genomic DNA is cleaved with two different restriction enzymes (a rare cutter and a frequent cutter); (2) short adapter sequences are ligated to the cut ends; (3) a subset of fragments is amplified by PCR using primers complementary to the adapters with selective nucleotides; (4) the amplified fragments are separated by electrophoresis and the banding pattern (fingerprint) is compared between individuals. AFLP needs no prior sequence information and detects many loci at once, but it is mainly dominant in nature.

subjective.topic: Genetic and Molecular Markers
subjective.question: What are SNP markers? Why are they considered important in crop improvement?
subjective.answer: SNPs (Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms) are variations at a single nucleotide position in the DNA sequence between individuals — for example one plant having A where another has G at the same position. They are the most abundant type of variation in the genome, are co-dominant and can be scored by automated, high-throughput methods. Because SNPs are thought to play a major role in producing phenotypic variation, they are widely used for genetic mapping, marker-assisted selection, variety identification and studying diversity in crops.

subjective.topic: Plant Tissue Culture — Basics and Technique
subjective.question: Define plant tissue culture. On what principle does regeneration of a whole plant from a single cell depend?
subjective.answer: Plant tissue culture is a set of in vitro techniques, methods and strategies — part of the group of technologies called plant biotechnology — in which small pieces of plant tissue (explants) are grown on a sterile nutrient medium under controlled conditions to regenerate whole plants. It works on the principle of TOTIPOTENCY: every living plant cell contains the complete genetic information of the plant and, given suitable nutrients and hormones, can be made totipotent and regenerate into a complete plant. This is why tissue culture produces clones — all the product cells have the same genotype.

subjective.topic: Plant Tissue Culture — Basics and Technique
subjective.question: Describe the basic steps of plant tissue culture.
subjective.answer: 1) Selection and preparation of the explant: a small piece of plant part or tissue is aseptically cut and used to initiate the culture. 2) Surface sterilization of the explant to remove microorganisms. 3) Inoculation: the explant is placed on a sterilized nutrient medium in a culture vessel. 4) Incubation under controlled conditions — typically 26–28 °C, light intensity of about 2000–4000 lux and a photoperiod of 16 hours light and 8 hours darkness. 5) Establishment and multiplication: the explant forms callus or shoots, which are sub-cultured for multiplication. 6) Root formation (rooting of shoots). 7) Hardening/acclimatization: plantlets are gradually adapted to outside conditions before transfer to soil.

subjective.topic: Plant Tissue Culture — Basics and Technique
subjective.question: What are the critical requirements for successful plant tissue culture?
subjective.answer: The critical requirements are: (1) aseptic (sterile) conditions throughout, because microorganisms grow much faster than plant cells on the rich medium and will overgrow the culture; (2) a suitable nutrient medium supplying minerals, vitamins, a carbon source and growth regulators; (3) clean, sterilized equipment and culture vessels; (4) proper surface sterilization of explants; and (5) controlled culture conditions of temperature, light intensity and photoperiod.

subjective.topic: Plant Tissue Culture — Basics and Technique
subjective.question: Write a note on the culture medium used in plant tissue culture, mentioning the MS medium.
subjective.answer: The culture medium provides all nutrients the growing tissue cannot make for itself: macronutrients and micronutrients, vitamins, a carbon source (usually sucrose), and plant growth regulators (auxins and cytokinins) in amounts chosen for the desired response. The artificial medium most widely used for tissue culture was introduced by Murashige and Skoog in 1962 (the MS medium). The medium is usually solidified with agar, its pH adjusted, and it is sterilized (commonly by autoclaving) before inoculation.

subjective.topic: Plant Tissue Culture — Basics and Technique
subjective.question: What is an explant? How is it prepared for culture?
subjective.answer: An explant is a small piece of a plant part or tissue that is aseptically cut and used to initiate a culture in a nutrient medium. Before inoculation the explant is surface-sterilized (e.g. with sodium hypochlorite or mercuric chloride solutions, then washed with sterile water) so that the culture starts free of microorganisms.

subjective.topic: Types of Culture, Regeneration and Micropropagation
subjective.question: What is callus culture? Give the role of callus in plant biotechnology.
subjective.answer: Callus is an unorganized mass of dividing parenchyma cells that forms when an explant is cultured on a medium containing suitable auxin. In callus culture, the callus is initiated from a selected explant and maintained by regular subculture. Role: callus is the starting material for cell suspension cultures, for regeneration of plants through organogenesis or somatic embryogenesis, for producing somaclonal variants, and for genetic transformation experiments, since single callus cells can be regenerated into whole plants.

subjective.topic: Types of Culture, Regeneration and Micropropagation
subjective.question: What is a cell suspension culture? How is the growth of a suspension culture monitored?
subjective.answer: A cell suspension culture consists of single cells and small cell aggregates growing dispersed in a liquid medium, usually initiated by transferring friable callus into agitated liquid medium. Its growth follows a typical growth curve (lag, exponential/log, linear and stationary phases). Growth is monitored by measuring parameters such as packed cell volume, fresh and dry weight, cell number and mitotic index at regular intervals. Suspension cultures are used for producing secondary metabolites, for somatic embryogenesis (as in carrot), and for protoplast and transformation work.

subjective.topic: Types of Culture, Regeneration and Micropropagation
subjective.question: Differentiate between organogenesis and embryogenesis as routes of plant regeneration in culture.
subjective.answer: Organogenesis is the formation of organs — shoots or roots — from cultured tissue. It may be direct (organs form straight from the explant) or indirect (organs form from an intervening callus). The balance of auxin and cytokinin controls it: auxins are involved in root initiation, while cytokinins promote shoot formation. Embryogenesis (somatic embryogenesis) is the formation of embryo-like structures (embryoids/somatic embryos) from somatic cells; these are bipolar structures with both shoot and root poles that develop into complete plantlets in one step, without separate rooting. Somatic embryogenesis gives a much higher propagation rate and is the basis of synthetic seeds, whereas organogenesis requires separate shoot-multiplication and rooting stages.

subjective.topic: Types of Culture, Regeneration and Micropropagation
subjective.question: What is micropropagation? Describe its stages and any three applications.
subjective.answer: Micropropagation is the practice of rapidly multiplying plant material in vitro to produce large numbers of identical plantlets. Stages: Stage 0 — selection and preparation of the mother plant; Stage I — establishment of the explant in culture; Stage II — multiplication of shoots; Stage III — rooting of shoots; Stage IV — acclimatization (hardening) and transfer to soil. Success depends on the genotype of the plant, the physiological status of the explant, the culture medium, light and temperature. Applications: (1) rapid mass production of elite, uniform plants throughout the year; (2) production of disease-free (virus-free) plants through meristem culture; (3) multiplication of species that are difficult to propagate by seed or are sterile; (4) conservation/storage of genetic resources in a small space.

subjective.topic: Plant Growth Regulators
subjective.question: Classify plant growth regulators and state the main function of each class.
subjective.answer: Plant growth regulators (PGRs) are classified into five main groups: 1) Auxins (e.g. IAA, NAA, 2,4-D) — promote cell elongation, root initiation and callus induction; also involved in geotropism. 2) Cytokinins (e.g. kinetin, BAP, zeatin) — promote cell division and shoot formation, and delay senescence. 3) Gibberellins (e.g. GA3) — promote stem elongation, seed germination and break dormancy. 4) Ethylene — a gaseous hormone promoting fruit ripening and senescence. 5) Abscisic acid (ABA) — promotes dormancy and stomatal closure and helps the plant respond to stress. In tissue culture, the relative amounts of auxin and cytokinin in the medium decide whether callus, roots or shoots are formed.

subjective.topic: Plant Growth Regulators
subjective.question: Write a note on the role of auxins in plant growth and in tissue culture.
subjective.answer: Auxins are growth regulators produced mainly in shoot tips and young leaves. They promote cell elongation, are involved in geotropism (bending of shoots and roots in response to gravity), initiate root formation, and maintain apical dominance. In tissue culture, auxins such as 2,4-D are used to induce callus, and auxins are specifically involved in root initiation when shoots are transferred to a rooting medium; embryogenesis in carrot suspension cultures is stimulated when auxin is withdrawn from the medium.

subjective.topic: Special Cultures: Anther, Protoplast, Embryo and Meristem Culture; Synthetic Seeds
subjective.question: What is anther culture? Write the applications of haploid plants in crop improvement.
subjective.answer: Anther culture is the in vitro culture of anthers (or isolated microspores/pollen) to produce haploid plants, because pollen grains carry only half the normal (haploid) number of chromosomes. Anthers with uninucleate pollen are generally suitable for culture, and embryoids can be induced, e.g. by cold pre-treatment of anthers at 3–5 °C for about 30 minutes; tobacco is the most successful example of anther/spore culture. Applications of haploids: (1) rapid development of pure homozygous lines after chromosome doubling, saving many generations of selfing; (2) easy selection of mutants, including disease-resistant mutants, because recessive genes are expressed directly; (3) transfer of desired alien genes; (4) induction of mutagenesis and genetic variability; and (5) development of aneuploids for genetic studies.

subjective.topic: Special Cultures: Anther, Protoplast, Embryo and Meristem Culture; Synthetic Seeds
subjective.question: What are protoplasts? How are they isolated, and what is somatic hybridization?
subjective.answer: Protoplasts are naked plant cells without the cell wall (the plasma membrane is the outermost boundary). Isolation is mainly by the enzymatic method: leaf or callus tissue is treated with cellulase and pectinase enzymes that digest the cell wall, followed by purification of the released protoplasts by filtration and centrifugation (a mechanical method also exists but gives low yields). Protoplasts of different species can be fused to generate a hybrid — this process is called somatic hybridization (protoplast fusion). It allows genes to be combined between species that cannot be crossed sexually, and is an important technique for overcoming barriers in wide hybridization and improving crops.

subjective.topic: Special Cultures: Anther, Protoplast, Embryo and Meristem Culture; Synthetic Seeds
subjective.question: What is embryo culture? What is embryo rescue and where is it used?
subjective.answer: Embryo culture is the in vitro culture of embryos on a nutrient medium. In embryo rescue — one of the earliest and most successful in vitro techniques — immature embryos from wide (interspecific or intergeneric) crosses, which would normally abort because the endosperm fails, are removed and grown in culture so the hybrid plant is saved. Embryo culture is also used to overcome seed dormancy, to shorten the breeding cycle, and to produce plants from seeds with no endosperm; mature embryo culture is the simpler form used when the embryo is fully developed.

subjective.topic: Special Cultures: Anther, Protoplast, Embryo and Meristem Culture; Synthetic Seeds
subjective.question: How does meristem (shoot tip) culture help in producing virus-free plants?
subjective.answer: The apical meristem of a plant is usually free of viruses even in an infected plant, because viruses move through vascular tissue and the meristem lacks developed vascular connections and divides faster than the virus spreads. Culturing the small meristem/shoot tip (under about 16 hours light at 25 °C) therefore regenerates plants free of the virus. Culture of meristems and single cells can thus be effectively used to eradicate pathogens from planting material. Meristem culture is also used for micropropagation and for storage of genetic resources.

subjective.topic: Special Cultures: Anther, Protoplast, Embryo and Meristem Culture; Synthetic Seeds
subjective.question: What are synthetic seeds? Give their advantages.
subjective.answer: Synthetic seeds are artificially encapsulated somatic embryos (also called encapsulated embryos) that functionally mimic true seeds and can develop into seedlings. The somatic embryo is coated, usually in a gel such as sodium alginate, which acts like a seed coat and may carry nutrients and protectants. Advantages: they can be produced in large numbers at any time of the year, allow clonal propagation of elite genotypes (including hybrids and sterile plants) in seed-like form, are easy to handle, store and transport, and can be sown directly like ordinary seed.

subjective.topic: Somaclonal Variation, Wide Hybridization and Germplasm Conservation
subjective.question: Define somaclonal variation. What are its causes?
subjective.answer: Somaclonal variation is the genetic variation found in plants regenerated from in vitro cultured cells and tissues (soma = somatic cells, clonal = from clones). Causes: (1) Physiological causes — prolonged culture and the action of growth regulators in the medium; (2) Genetic causes — gene mutation, activation of transposable elements, changes in DNA sequence and chromosomal changes (altered chromosome number/structure), which is why regenerated plants with chromosomal changes often show changes in leaf shape and colour, growth rate and habit, and sexual fertility; (3) Biochemical causes — changes in the biochemical environment of cultured cells. Variation increases with the length of the culture period.

subjective.topic: Somaclonal Variation, Wide Hybridization and Germplasm Conservation
subjective.question: Write the applications of somaclonal variation in crop improvement.
subjective.answer: Somaclonal variation is a useful source of novel variability: several novel variants of existing crops have been developed through it (e.g. pure thorn-less variants). Its applications include production of agronomically useful plants, resistance to diseases, resistance to abiotic stresses (drought, salinity), resistance to herbicides, and improved seed quality — all without introducing foreign genes.

subjective.topic: Somaclonal Variation, Wide Hybridization and Germplasm Conservation
subjective.question: What is wide hybridization? Discuss the barriers to wide crosses and the techniques used to overcome them.
subjective.answer: Wide hybridization is crossing between different species or genera to introduce new genetic variation — a critical requirement for crop improvement, e.g. transferring disease resistance from a wild relative into a cultivated crop. Barriers: pre-zygotic barriers prevent fertilization (pollen fails to germinate or the pollen tube cannot reach the ovule), and post-zygotic barriers act after fertilization (hybrid embryo aborts, or the hybrid is sterile). Techniques to overcome them: (1) in vitro fertilization for pre-zygotic barriers; (2) protoplast fusion (somatic hybridization) to bypass sexual crossing altogether; (3) embryo rescue/culture to save aborting hybrid embryos; (4) use of a bridging species; (5) backcrossing; and (6) doubling of chromosomes to restore fertility of the hybrid.

subjective.topic: Somaclonal Variation, Wide Hybridization and Germplasm Conservation
subjective.question: What is germplasm conservation? Differentiate between in-situ and ex-situ preservation.
subjective.answer: Germplasm conservation is the preservation of the genetic material (seeds, tissues or plants) of a species so that its genetic diversity is not lost. In-situ preservation means conserving the plants in their natural habitat (e.g. protected areas and gene sanctuaries), where they continue to evolve. Ex-situ preservation means conserving them outside their habitat — in seed banks, field gene banks, or in vitro. In vitro approaches include cryopreservation (storage at very low temperature, e.g. in liquid nitrogen or with solid carbon dioxide at −79 °C), cold storage, and low-pressure/low-oxygen storage, which give germplasm with a good survival rate and are especially useful for clonal crops whose seeds are not the best material to conserve.

subjective.topic: Plant Transformation and Transgenic Technology
subjective.question: Define transformation and competence. How are bacterial cells made competent to take up foreign DNA?
subjective.answer: Transformation is the process by which a cell takes up foreign (exogenous) DNA from its environment and incorporates it; transformation occurs naturally in bacteria. Competence is the state of being able to take up exogenous DNA from the environment. Only about 1% of bacterial species are naturally competent under laboratory conditions, so artificial competence is induced by: (1) the calcium chloride method — chilling treatment in the presence of divalent cations such as Ca2+ (in CaCl2) makes the cell membrane permeable to plasmid DNA, followed by a brief heat shock; (2) electroporation — short electric pulses create temporary pores in the membrane; and (3) the heat shock method. Transformed cells are then selected, e.g. on a medium containing an antibiotic such as ampicillin or kanamycin if the plasmid carries the corresponding resistance gene.

subjective.topic: Plant Transformation and Transgenic Technology
subjective.question: Describe Agrobacterium-mediated transformation of plants, explaining the roles of the Ti plasmid, T-DNA, vir genes and opines.
subjective.answer: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a soil bacterium that induces crown gall disease in plants and is the most preferred method for plant transformation. It carries the Ti (tumour-inducing) plasmid; a part of this plasmid, the T-DNA, is transferred into the plant cell and integrated into the plant genome. The vir (virulence) genes of the plasmid control this transfer: they are activated by phenolic compounds released from wounded plant explants. In the natural system the T-DNA genes make the plant produce opines and agropines, which the bacterium uses as sources of carbon and energy. For genetic engineering, the tumour-causing genes are removed from the T-DNA and replaced with the desired gene plus a selectable marker; the bacterium then delivers the useful gene into the plant cell, and transformed cells are regenerated into transgenic plants. (In octopine strains the Ti plasmid has two T-DNA regions, TL of about 14 kb and TR of about 7 kb.)

subjective.topic: Plant Transformation and Transgenic Technology
subjective.question: Compare vector-mediated and direct methods of gene transfer in plants, giving examples.
subjective.answer: Vector-mediated gene transfer uses a biological vector to carry the gene into the plant cell — the main example is Agrobacterium-mediated transfer using the Ti plasmid; viruses also act as natural vectors for genetic engineering. Direct (vector-less) methods deliver DNA physically or chemically: the gene gun (biolistics, DNA-coated particles shot into cells), electroporation, microinjection, lipofection (efficient for transferring genes into animal and plant cells), and the calcium phosphate method, in which DNA mixed with calcium chloride solution and isotonic phosphate buffer forms a DNA–calcium phosphate precipitate that cells take up. Agrobacterium-mediated transfer is the most preferred method because it is simple, gives stable integration and usually low copy number.

subjective.topic: Plant Transformation and Transgenic Technology
subjective.question: What is blue-white screening? Explain the role of the lacZ gene in it.
subjective.answer: Blue-white screening is a visual method to identify bacterial colonies that carry a recombinant plasmid. The vector carries the lacZ gene, which codes for the α-subunit (alpha peptide) of the enzyme β-galactosidase. On a medium containing X-gal, colonies with an intact lacZ gene produce functional β-galactosidase and turn blue. When a foreign gene is inserted into the lacZ region, the gene is disrupted, β-galactosidase is not produced, and the recombinant colonies remain white. Thus white colonies are the ones containing the desired recombinant plasmid.

subjective.topic: Plant Transformation and Transgenic Technology
subjective.question: How are transformed cells selected after gene transfer? What problem is associated with the primary transplastomic event?
subjective.answer: Selection is done with a selectable marker gene carried on the same vector as the gene of interest — most commonly an antibiotic resistance gene: only transformed cells grow on a medium containing that antibiotic (e.g. ampicillin or kanamycin), while untransformed cells die. Reporter genes such as lacZ (blue-white screening) are also used to check colonies. In plastid transformation, the primary transplastomic event results in heteroplasmic cells — cells containing a mixture of transformed and untransformed plastids — so repeated rounds of selection are needed to obtain uniformly transformed (homoplasmic) plants.

subjective.topic: Plant Responses to Biotic and Abiotic Stress
subjective.question: Describe the responses of plants to biotic stress caused by pathogens.
subjective.answer: Plants respond to attack by fungi, bacteria and viruses both physically and chemically. Physical responses include strengthening and cross-linking of cell wall proteins and deposition of lignin and callose to block pathogen entry and spread; physical blockage in xylem vessels, however, prevents water and mineral translocation and causes wilting. Chemical responses include production of pathogenesis-related (PR) proteins, phytoalexins and saponins (glycosylated compounds — triterpenoids, steroids or steroidal glycoalkaloids — with antimicrobial action). At the physiological level, diseased plants show increased respiration, reduced photosynthesis (e.g. because of fungal toxins such as tabtoxin and tentoxin) and increased transpiration; in necrotrophy the pathogen kills the plant cells outright. Viruses are obligate parasites (e.g. tobacco mosaic virus) and spread from plant to plant through wounds, vectors and vegetative propagation.

subjective.topic: Plant Responses to Biotic and Abiotic Stress
subjective.question: Write a note on the physiological effects of abiotic stresses (salt and heavy metals) on plants.
subjective.answer: Salt stress damages plants physiologically by disturbing water uptake (osmotic effect) and by ion toxicity, reducing growth and yield. Heavy metals cause toxicity symptoms when their concentration in the soil is elevated: both essential heavy metals (needed in traces) and non-essential ones such as mercury (Hg) and chromium (Cr) can become toxic. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced under stresses such as light stress and act as signalling molecules for activating defence responses. Environmental stresses are economically important — for example, about 50% of crop yield in Pakistan is affected by wind stress.

subjective.topic: Plant Responses to Biotic and Abiotic Stress
subjective.question: How has biotechnology helped to safeguard crops against diseases?
subjective.answer: Biotechnology safeguards crops against disease in several ways: (1) molecular diagnostics are used in agriculture to diagnose crop and livestock diseases accurately and at an early stage, so control measures can be applied in time; (2) tissue culture of single cells and meristems eradicates pathogens from planting material, giving disease-free stock; (3) genetic engineering and marker-assisted breeding develop varieties resistant to fungi, bacteria and viruses; and (4) somaclonal variation and wide hybridization are used to create and transfer new disease resistance into cultivated crops.
